articles.title: Mosque set on fire in Israel, politicians blame Netanyahu’s ‘incitement’
articles.summary: Knesset MPs call the incident ‘a hate crime’ while Hamas blames Israeli ‘settler gangs’.
articles.body:
Police are investigating after a mosque was set on fire in al-Dahi, a village in northern Israel where Palestinian citizens of Israel live.

The attack near the city of Afula on Thursday came after a car-ramming late on Wednesday targeted another city that is home to Palestinian citizens of Israel.

A slate of politicians have blamed the mosque attack on “incitement” by the camp of caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

“An investigation has been opened into the suspected arson of a room in the lower part of a mosque in the village of al-Dahi and the spraying of graffiti on a nearby street,” police said in a statement.

“The Israel Police takes any attempt to harm religious symbols very seriously and will act decisively and without compromise to bring the suspects to justice,” they added.

The mosque’s imam, Khaled al-Zoubi, said he had seen “smoke and a fire” when he arrived for dawn prayer on Thursday.

“We came to the mosque, and there was smoke and fire burning from the bottom part of the mosque,” he said, explaining that the mosque has two floors.

“Three masked individuals came from the woods on the mountain we have here; they tried to enter the inside of the mosque, the first floor, but there was an iron gate there, so they couldn’t get in.

“They went down from this area, entered, and broke the window of the mosque’s ground floor, and they had an incendiary bottle with them; they threw it, of course, and burned the mosque from below,” he recounted.

Senior Hamas official Abdul Rahman Shadid said attackers set fire to the mosque early on Thursday and wrote racist slogans on its walls. Photos from the AFP news agency showed graffiti reading “revenge” scrawled on the walls of buildings near the mosque.

“Setting a mosque on fire is a heinous hate crime. This is not Jewish and it is not Israeli,” said Yair Lapid, a leading member of the anti-Netanyahu bloc.

“The rampant incitement against Arab Israelis must stop,” he wrote on X, pointing to Netanyahu’s right-wing camp.

Yair Golan, who heads the left-leaning Democrats party , described the incident as “Jewish terrorism”.

“It is the consequence of the campaign of incitement Netanyahu and his government are waging against Arab citizens of Israel,” he said.

The head of the Arab-majority Joint List, Youssef Jabareen, visited the village of al-Dahi on Thursday.

“We hold Netanyahu and his entire cabinet, and all the extremists with him, responsible for translating their dangerous incitement into reality through attacks on our people,” said Jabareen.

Mansour Abbas, a member of Israel’s Knesset and Ra’am chairman, also condemned the attack.

“A hate crime, an act of terror, and the desecration of a holy place. This is not an isolated incident, but a direct result of the far right’s incitement campaign against Arab citizens,” he said. “I call on Prime Minister Netanyahu – stop the incitement. Granting legitimacy to violence endangers human life.”

Hamas condemned the attack that it blamed on “ settler gangs ”.

The attack reflects “the scale of organised terrorism carried out by extremist settler militias under the protection of the right-wing occupation government,” Hamas official Shadid said.

He added that such attacks were intended to “displace our people and empty the land of its inhabitants” through killing, burning and intimidation.

The attack came shortly after Israeli police arrested a man suspected of carrying out a ramming attack in Kaf Qasim, another city where Palestinian citizens of Israel live, late on Wednesday.

Eight people were injured in that attack. A Palestinian civil society organisation said the suspect is an Israeli settler. Police also said they had opened an investigation.

articles.title: Florida pastor convicted in Haitian president's assassination plot funded partly by US COVID relief money
articles.summary: Christian Emmanuel Sanon was convicted in the plot to kill Haitian President Jovenel Moïse, a scheme prosecutors say was hatched in South Florida.
articles.body: A Florida pastor was convicted Wednesday in a plot to assassinate Haitian President Jovenel Moïse that prosecutors say was hatched in South Florida and partly financed with U.S. COVID-19 relief money used to pay foreign mercenaries. Christian Emmanuel Sanon, a dual Haitian-American citizen, was found guilty on all eight federal charges following a nearly eight-week trial in Miami. He faces up to life in prison when he is sentenced Feb. 10. Prosecutors said conspirators initially planned to install Sanon as Haiti's president in exchange for lucrative security and infrastructure contracts before abandoning him as their preferred candidate weeks ahead of the assassination. FLORIDA JURY CONVICTS 4 MEN WHO PLOTTED ASSASSINATION OF HAITI'S PRESIDENT FROM SOUTH FLORIDA HUB A squad of mostly retired Colombian soldiers stormed Moïse's home on July 7, 2021, killing the president and wounding his wife. Sanon denied knowing about any plan to kill Moïse, testifying that he had communicated with people seeking to replace the Haitian leader but that the group had moved on to another candidate long before the assassination. His attorney, Zeljka Bozanic, said the defense team was disappointed by the verdict and planned to appeal. According to prosecutors, South Florida served as a hub for planning and financing the conspiracy, which involved roughly two dozen foreign mercenaries paid in part with money obtained from federal pandemic relief programs intended to help businesses. The indictment said the scheme took shape in April 2021, when Sanon met with a former Haitian senator and several U.S. businesspeople in South Florida. 'THEY FED HIM HIS OWN EARS': TOP REPUBLICAN SHARES HORRIFYING STORIES OF GANG RULE IN HAITI Investigators said the group agreed that Sanon, once installed as president, would award contracts for infrastructure projects, security forces and military equipment to two Florida-based companies. The companies initially hired about 18 Colombians with military training to provide security for Sanon. Conspirators also spent months acquiring weapons and body armor and attempting to establish ties with Haitian gangs, prosecutors said. Prosecutors presented evidence that Sanon helped raise money for the conspiracy and arranged travel and lodging in Haiti for himself and others. BUKELE WARNS HAITIAN GANG LEADERS THAT HIS FORCES WILL 'FINISH' THEM AS HE DID IN EL SALVADOR By June 2021, however, the plotters concluded Sanon lacked the constitutional qualifications and popular support needed to become president and shifted their backing to another candidate. Sanon is among a dozen defendants convicted in the U.S. investigation into Moïse's assassination, with more than 40 people charged and five already serving life sentences. Four other men were convicted in May of conspiring to kill or kidnap Moïse, providing material support for the plot and violating the U.S. Neutrality Act. They also face possible life sentences. articles.title: Phil, the bar-tailed godwit, tracked in epic migration
articles.summary: A bird has astonished conservationists by completing a 6,800-mile round trip to Siberia and back.
articles.body:
A bird named Phil has astonished conservationists by completing a 6,800-mile (10,900km) round trip from England's east coast to Siberia and back.

Bar-tailed godwits are champion fliers, migrating between Britain and the Arctic, but the precise routes used by individual birds is largely unknown.

Phil was fitted with a tiny solar-powered tracker that recorded his movements throughout the journey.

The data showed he travelled from The Wash to the Wadden Sea, along the coasts of the Netherlands, Germany and Denmark, before continuing to Siberia.

On his return, he crossed the Arctic Ocean to northern Norway, stopping on three islands before heading back through the Wadden Sea to The Wash.

Scientists say Phil's extraordinary travels highlight the importance of protecting the world's wetlands, which are havens for millions of migratory birds each year.

Dr Nigel Clark, of the conservation charity, The Wash Wader Research Group, said The Wash is the UK's single most important coastal wetland for migratory waders, with spectacular numbers seen in autumn and winter.

"Tracking birds like Phil the Godwit shows us how connected the Wash is with the rest of the flyway," he said.

Jeff Kew, RSPB Coastal Advisor, said many migratory bird species cross borders, depending on a whole network of wetlands along the way.

That's why it's so important to look after these special places."

Bar-tailed godwits are wading birds of similar size to pigeons, but with long bills and legs.

They are regarded as one of nature's long-distance endurance athletes, with one subspecies making the longest known non-stop migration of any bird, flying 8,425 miles (13,559km) from Alaska to New Zealand.

Phil's journey included a handful of stops to rest and refuel.

He will now spend the winter relaxing with thousands of other wading birds at the Snettisham Nature Reserve in Norfolk.

articles.title: Fighting global warming without naming its biggest driver? COP31 draft drops mention of fossil fuels
articles.summary: The world came together to fight climate change, but the latest draft agreement at its biggest climate summit has found no place for the biggest driver of
articles.body: The world came together to fight climate change, but the latest draft agreement at its biggest climate summit has found no place for the biggest driver of global warming.COP31's revised draft, released on Thursday, has dropped all references to fossil fuels, including a proposal for accelerated action to phase out coal, oil and gas, triggering fresh concerns over the summit's ability to secure stronger climate commitments.According to AFP, Australia, which is co-hosting the summit and steering the negotiations, released the revised text after days of tense consultations in Antalya, Turkey. The document is nearly half the length of an earlier draft and makes no explicit mention of coal, oil or gas.The removal reflects deep divisions among participating countries over commitments to reduce dependence on fossil fuels. While several nations have pushed for stronger language on phasing out coal, oil and gas, others remain reluctant to accept commitments that could affect their energy security and economies.Despite the removal of fossil fuel references, the revised draft retains proposals on electrification and climate adaptation finance. It calls for increasing the share of global final energy demand met by electricity to 35 percent by 2035, a key initiative of summit host Turkey. The proposal says greater electrification could strengthen energy security while reducing greenhouse gas emissions.The disagreement comes two years after countries agreed at COP28 in Dubai to transition away from fossil fuels. However, last year's summit in Brazil ended without any mention of fossil fuels in its final agreement, prompting several countries to push for stronger language at the Antalya meeting.The divide between developed and developing nations has further complicated negotiations, particularly over climate finance.Developing countries are demanding greater financial support from industrialised nations to tackle climate-related disasters and adapt to rising temperatures.Developed nations, however, have resisted calls for increased funding, citing budget constraints and arguing that major emerging economies should also share the financial responsibility.The draft also proposes further discussions on tripling climate adaptation finance by 2035, addressing a key demand from developing nations. It expresses "deep concern" over the imminent breach of the 1.5°C temperature goal set under the Paris Agreement and underscores the importance of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).Meanwhile, Panama has threatened to block any final agreement that does not address its demands, including a proposal to cap global oil production. The warning adds another hurdle to negotiations, with nearly 200 countries facing a Friday deadline to reach a consensus on the final climate deal.The summit is unfolding amid a difficult global backdrop, with a record-breaking El Nino, climate-related disasters across regions from Europe to Nepal and a global energy shock triggered by the Iran war. These developments have added urgency to negotiations over energy security, climate finance and global emissions cuts.

articles.title: Canada’s beloved Tim Hortons brews ire over ‘excessive’ Israeli data deal
articles.summary: Advocates raised concerns about consumer privacy and data-sharing, involving a firm with ties to Israel’s military.
articles.body:
When Canadians order their morning cup of joe using the coffeehouse chain Tim Hortons app, coffee may not be the only thing being delivered. Users’ sensitive personal data could also be travelling across the world – to an Israeli cybertech company.

The beloved nationwide chain has found itself at the centre of an angry backlash over consumer privacy and its ties to Forter, the Israeli firm.

On Tuesday, Canadians for Justice and Peace in the Middle East (CPJME) revealed that the Tim Hortons app has been sending “sensitive user data” to Forter. Al Jazeera has independently confirmed that the app does share user data with Forter.

CPJME also raised concerns about Forter’s founders’ links to an Israeli military intelligence unit accused of mass surveillance of Palestinians, as well as the unit’s reported association with Lavender, an artificial intelligence (AI) system used to generate lists of Palestinians to be targeted during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza .

The group’s findings build on an investigation by Canadian broadcaster CBC reported last week, examining the data-sharing practices of some of the country’s most popular apps. But the investigation did not identify which company was receiving Tim Hortons users’ data or disclose where it was based.

Neither Tim Hortons nor its parent company, Restaurant Brands International (RBI), had responded to Al Jazeera’s queries by the time of publication. Forter had also not responded to Al Jazeera’s queries.

Tim Hortons told CBC that the data-sharing arrangement is a fraud-prevention measure. However, experts have described the extent of the data collected as overly intrusive.

“The collection occurs prior to consent, and in my view is excessive,” Joel Reardon, a computer science professor at the University of Calgary whose research underpinned the CBC investigation, told Al Jazeera.

CPJME, meanwhile, warned that the practice could expose consumers to privacy risks that extend far beyond the original purpose of fraud prevention.

“What concerns us is that there is this massive … digital footprint being built of people through these apps, seemingly without their knowledge, in the name of preventing fraud, and that data is flowing to an Israeli cybertech company whose operations … [are] opaque to us and [who] have concerning ties,” Jason Toney, CJPME’s director of media advocacy, told Al Jazeera.

During its investigation, CBC found that the apps it examined, including Tim Hortons’, disclose that they collect or share certain data. However, experts questioned whether the amount of information gathered was proportionate to the simple act of buying a cup of coffee.

CBC found that the app appeared to send data to the third-party company right when it launches. This data includes unique identifiers, sensor details and the names of nearby Wi-Fi networks, which Reardon said can be used to determine a person’s location.

“I’m usually troubled by the precise ongoing location data collection because that can reveal a great deal of information about an individual,” said Reardon.

He explained that Forter gathers enough information from the Tim Hortons app to create a digital fingerprint for each device, so it can be identified in the future.

That is concerning for OpenMedia, a Canadian organisation advocating for digital rights, privacy and consumer protection.

“People open the Tim Hortons app to order a coffee, not have their data, including location indicators, exported to foreign companies,” its executive director, Matt Hatfield, told Al Jazeera.

But he said Tim Hortons is not unusual in doing this. “Many companies quietly pass data to a long chain of vendors that customers have never heard of and never chose.”

“We effectively create these chains of trust that our data is handled appropriately – where any company along the chain can breach and abuse our data,” Hatfield said.

Tim Hortons told CBC that the third party it works with – Forter – is not allowed to sell the data it collects through its app and that the coffee chain itself does not sell users’ personal information.

But Reardon said effective fraud prevention can be carried out without collecting data giving users’ precise locations.

“It is useful to be clear if Tim Hortons is talking about protecting [themselves] from fraud, or if they [are] protecting the users,” the researcher added.

Forter’s founders have previously told media that the data it receives is used to protect “wealthy corporations” from fraudulent activity, Toney noted. “If a consumer’s credit card is fraudulently used, for example, to purchase something online, it’s usually the wealthy corporations that are on the hook for reimbursing that funding,” he explained.

“So they use Forter to avoid having to take on those costs … It’s not really about protecting ordinary consumers, at least that’s not how they have framed it publicly in the past.”

Beyond the companies handling the data, there are questions about whether consumers understand what they are agreeing to. The Tim Hortons app, in its user policies, states that when customers use it, they agree to its terms.

“Research shows that consumers are frequently unaware of the particulars they consent to when accepting a privacy policy,” Johanna Gunawan, an assistant professor of computer science and law at Maastricht University, told Al Jazeera.

Such policies are lengthy and often not conveyed in plain language, she said.

“The cognitive load to understand the full privacy implications of acceptance is frequently imbalanced against the relative ease or speed of providing agreement,” explained Gunawan.

Questions about the app’s data practices do not end with what information is collected or whether users consent to sharing it. They also extend to the company receiving that data.

Forter’s founders – Michael Reitblat, Liron Damri and Alon Shemesh – are all alumni of the Israeli military’s Unit 8200, its signals intelligence and cyberwarfare division, The Times of Israel has reported. The company’s technology is enhanced by Israeli military intelligence, The Jerusalem Post reported in 2018.

Last year, Microsoft barred the Israeli military from some of its services following an investigation which found that Unit 8200 used its Azure cloud computing platform to store phone call data obtained through mass surveillance of Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.

The division has also been associated with Lavender , the AI technology that Israel has created to target Palestinians during its genocidal war on Gaza.

While the ties are “concerning”, said CPJME’s Toney, he cautioned against speculating whether Forter uses data collected through the Tim Hortons app in a “nefarious” manner. There is no evidence of this, and he added that the Israeli firm appears to be well established.

On its website, Forter says it works on fraud prevention for many high-profile companies, ranging from eBay to Shein, Reebok and LG Electronics.

Al Jazeera was not able to confirm whether Forter still uses Israeli military intelligence or whether any data it holds is accessible to the Israeli government or military agencies.

This is not the first time Tim Hortons has landed in hot water over its handling of user data.

In 2022, Canadian federal and provincial privacy commissioners found that the company’s app had illegally tracked users’ locations through a third-party provider, even when the app was closed.

Tim Hortons faced no fines then because Canada’s privacy regulator cannot issue them, said OpenMedia’s Hatfield.

He said Canada’s privacy laws are insufficient and outdated.

“Our federal private-sector privacy law, PIPEDA, is more than 25 years old. Under it, a company can send your data to a service provider without asking you, as long as it says it remains ‘accountable’ for that data,” said Hatfield, referring to Canada’s Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act.

“In practice, Canadians often can’t find out who receives their data, which country it ends up in, or which foreign laws or governments might be able to reach it.”

He said companies should be telling their customers this directly and respecting their stated preferences for how their data is used.

Bill C-36, the government’s new proposed privacy legislation introduced in June this year, meanwhile, “would only partially help”, said the digital rights advocate.

“It would require a privacy impact assessment before data leaves Canada, and it would introduce real financial penalties,” said Hatfield. “But it still lets companies hand data to service providers without consent, and those providers would only be directly bound by its security and breach-reporting rules.”

More worryingly, he added, the bill places privacy enforcement under a new regulator, which will be required to consider factors beyond privacy, including Canada’s trade agreements, economic growth and the broader public interest, before launching an investigation into a privacy violation.

“In practice, this may mean that while privacy violations may be more clearly illegal once C-36 passes, the Canadian government could pressure the regulator to ignore violations associated with close trade partners,” said Hatfield.

Despite the results of its last investigation, CPJME is now calling for another inquiry by the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada to look into the handling of consumer data by Tim Hortons, said Toney.

Al Jazeera contacted the privacy commissioner’s office about this but did not receive a response.

Toney’s organisation has also filed a complaint with the CBC’s ombudsperson, citing violations in journalistic standards and practices for failing to disclose Forter’s identity in its own investigation.

“CBC’s reporting obscures the true scale of the privacy risk Tim Hortons has exposed its users to. CBC is letting Tim Hortons and Forter off the hook. Canadians deserve to understand the truth,” said Toney.

Maastricht University’s Gunawan said she also believes companies should take responsibility for the privacy and security practices of third-party technology providers.

“That’s simple transparency and due diligence,” she said.

Hatfield said: “Questions about a vendor’s ties to any foreign military or intelligence service are legitimate and deserve clear answers. The same standard should apply whether the vendor is American, Chinese, Israeli or Canadian.”

At minimum, said Hatfield, Tim Hortons should publicly name every third party that receives data from its app and explain why it sends that data. The company should also disclose where the data is stored, and who can access it.

“And frankly, it shouldn’t be giving our data to anyone when its business is selling coffee and doughnuts!”

articles.title: Ukraine strikes Putin’s prized Crimean bridge for third time in a week
articles.summary: Ukraine struck the bridge linking Russia and Crimea for the third time in a week, forcing a suspension of train services across it, Russian authorities said.
articles.body: Ukraine struck the bridge linking Russia and Crimea for the third time in a week, forcing a suspension of train services across it, Russian authorities said, hours before President Vladimir Putin met the leaders of China and the U.S. The timing and impact of Ukraine‘s attacks on the bridge, the longest in Europe and a symbol of Putin’s Russia, are awkward for the Kremlin chief as he participates in what Moscow has cast as a historic trilateral summit with President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Moscow hopes the meeting will send a signal to allies and foes that it — rather than the European Union and Britain — is part of an emerging new multilateral world order. There was no immediate comment on the latest attack from Ukraine or Volodymyr Zelenskyy, its president, who was due to hold talks in Berlin later on Thursday with U.S. peace envoys. Sergei Aksyonov, Crimea’s Russian-installed governor, issued a defiant video message in which he said rail travel across the bridge would resume later on Thursday. “We have the strength, the resolve and the understanding of how to resolve this situation. We will overcome everything. Crimea is with Russia forever!” Aksyonov said. In a statement, Russia’s transport ministry said that nobody had been hurt in the latest Ukrainian attack on the Black Sea peninsula, which Moscow annexed from Ukraine in 2014, and that specialists were assessing damage to the bridge. The 12-mile bridge is a flagship project that Putin inaugurated in 2018 and that symbolizes Russia’s attachment to the peninsula, which is also the home of its Black Sea Fleet, whose ships Ukraine has repeatedly targeted. On Tuesday, Ukrainian drones and missiles destroyed the central road section of the Crimean Bridge, forcing its main road arch to crumble into the sea while leaving a yawning gap, according to videos and images verified by Reuters, dealing a military and symbolic blow to Russia. That attack is likely to make it harder for Russia to keep up supplies to the peninsula, which is home to nearly 2.5 million people, and is likely to put pressure on Russian military logistics in parts of southern Ukraine held by Moscow’s forces. This week‘s first attack, on Monday, caused more minor damage to the bridge.

articles.title: Raise the Colours founder says Birmingham flag injunction case 'spiralling out of control'
articles.summary: Birmingham City Council says the flags pose a hazard and fuel community tensions.
articles.body:
The co-founder of anti-migrant group Raise the Colours has said an interim injunction banning him and others from putting flags on lamp-posts in Birmingham is "spiralling out of control", as he learned the case could go to trial.

The High Court granted Birmingham City Council the order on Wednesday against Ryan Bridge and others, after thousands of union jacks and St George's flags were put up across the city.

The council argued that they posed a hazard on lamp-posts, signs and other highway structures, and fuelled community tensions.

On Thursday, Bridge attended another hearing where he was told the injunction had come into force and would be in place until a trial or further court order.

The 45-year-old heard that if the council sought a permanent injunction, the case could involve at least three to four days of evidence.

He said: "It's spiralling out of control, isn't it?" and added that he did not "want to exploit any more of the public purse and the council's money".

Bridge, from Blackwell, near Bromsgrove in Worcestershire, said he stopped putting up flags in Birmingham when he first heard about the injunction.

He said the other defendants in the case, which include six other named individuals and "persons unknown" who may put up flags, thought the case was "done".

One of the other named defendants in the case, Billy Allison, who is an activist with Raise the Colours, was found guilty of murder on Wednesday after punching a man in the neck on a dance floor in Lichfield, Staffordshire.

The court heard on Thursday there was not "much point" in pursuing the civil claim against Allison because he faced a mandatory life sentence.

Judge Emma Kelly said the interim injunction was "not the court nor the claimant 'banning the union jack' or the display of Pride flags or anything of the like".

She added that the court would encourage the parties to reach a resolution without going to trial.

A Freedom of Information request published earlier this week showed that the council spent almost £170,000 this year, up to the end of October, removing unauthorised flags from public infrastructure.

The maximum sentence for breaching a civil injunction is two years in prison.

Bridge asked for clarification on what amounted to "encouragement" under the injunction, saying he was concerned about how it could be interpreted.

He told the court: "If I say 'your flag looks nice' I could be encouraging somebody and go to jail for two years.

"It's quite worrying for me and regular everyday people."

Kelly said the term was routinely included in injunctions and that whether something amounted to encouragement would depend on the circumstances of each case.

The court also heard the council's injunction application included reports of alleged intimidation, harassment and obstruction linked to flags being put up in the city.

Kelly said the court would encourage the parties to reach a resolution without going to trial.

She added that the interim injunction was "not the court nor the claimant 'banning the union jack' or the display of Pride flags or anything of the like".

The order covers flags of all types but relates only to unauthorised flags attached to street furniture in Birmingham.

articles.title: Covid Inquiry: UK should co-ordinate its response with the Republic of Ireland in future
articles.summary: In its latest report into the programme of test and trace, it said cooperation was needed "to ensure that border control measures are effective and operable in practice".
articles.body:
The UK should coordinate its response to any future pandemic with the Republic of Ireland because of the added complexity of disease control across the Irish border, the Covid-19 inquiry has said.

In its latest 'Test, trace and isolate' report into the programme of test and trace, it said cooperation was needed "to ensure that border control measures are effective and operable in practice".

During the pandemic, Northern Ireland chose to align its international border control measures with the UK rather than with the Republic.

Inquiry chair Baroness Heather Hallett said despite this decision, there was close liaison between the UK government, devolved administrations and the Irish government.

In addition, in May 2020 the Northern Ireland Executive announced it would develop its own contact tracing app rather than adopt the one in development in England.

It used the same technology and provider as the Republic of Ireland and the cross border apps were the "first in the world to achieve interoperability", the report said.

"The Northern Ireland Executive entered into a Memorandum of Understanding with the Irish government on 7 April 2020 to allow regular data-sharing and the sharing of information on international travel policies," said the inquiry report.

This included weekly meetings between the two governments' health departments and the sharing of data in relation to the trajectory of the pandemic and information about international travel policy.

It also involved working closely together in order to inform policies about border control.

"The complexity of relations between the four nations, together with the additional complexity arising from the land border between Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland, must be carefully examined and addressed in the development of any future border control approach."

The report also said both sides of the Irish border were left open to potential infection risk because of the lower level of measures put in place by the UK government.

"By April 2020, 93% of countries and territories had put measures in place – such as flight suspensions, border closures and travel restrictions – to control their international borders," said the report.

By contrast, it said, the UK government only requested (rather than directed) travellers from Wuhan, China, to self-isolate in January 2020 and travellers from some other high-risk areas to self-isolate in February 2020.

"This did not prevent a coachload of tourists from Wuhan entering the UK and travelling from England to Scotland and then to Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland in February 2020.

"The UK government implemented no further border control measures until June 2020."

The inquiry found that the test and trace system was in part successful in Northern Ireland.

Despite having only 78 tracers trained by May 2020, the programme worked effectively because it operated from a centralised office.

"The team adopted a specific strategy that emphasised being personable and convivial in their interactions.

"By June 2020, 92% of people who had tested positive for Covid-19 and those who had been in close contact with them were reached within 24 hours," said the report.

It said the centralised system worked in Northern Ireland because its population is relatively small and it has a single, comparatively small healthcare system that enabled flexibility and a more rapid response.

"The scale of its system meant that it was able to replicate some of the advantages typically associated with local teams."

The inquiry report also found Northern Ireland was successful in the operation of payment entitlements to people self-isolating because it differed from other parts of the UK in using an existing Discretionary Support scheme.

On a UK-wide basis, Baroness Hallett said failings in testing and tracing left the UK "effectively blind" to how quickly Covid was spreading early in the pandemic.

"The UK was simply not prepared. Too many lives were cut short," she said.

Campaign group Covid-19 Bereaved Families for Justice UK said the inquiry has "exposed the lies and incompetence that left thousands of us grieving loved ones who should still be here".

The group said the government failures, such as the slow testing rate and sidelining of local public health teams "cost lives".

articles.title: Japan to conduct first-ever live-fire military drills in India, test surface-to-ship missiles
articles.summary: India and Japan have agreed to allow the Japan Self-Defence Forces (JSDF) to conduct live-fire training at firing ranges in India for the first time,
articles.body: India and Japan have agreed to allow the Japan Self-Defence Forces (JSDF) to conduct live-fire training at firing ranges in India for the first time, including exercises involving surface-to-ship missiles. The decision was announced on Thursday, November 19, after the fourth India-Japan 2+2 Foreign and Defence Ministerial Meeting in Tokyo. Both sides signed a Letter of Intent (LoI) on the use of Indian firing ranges and agreed to speed up coordination between their defence authorities to implement the plan.The move marks a significant step in defence cooperation between the two countries, with both sides looking to expand military exercises, strengthen maritime security and deepen collaboration in advanced defence technologies.Defence minister Rajnath Singh and external affairs minister S Jaishankar co-chaired the meeting with their Japanese counterparts, foreign minister Toshimitsu Motegi and defence minister Shinjiro Koizumi.Japan, India look to deepen defence cooperationThe joint statement issued after the meeting highlighted growing strategic convergence between the two countries amid an increasingly uncertain global security environment.The ministers welcomed the expansion of bilateral military exercises. Japan Air Self-Defence Force fighter aircraft participated for the first time in the India-Japan Air Force exercise, Veer Guardian 26, held in India. Both sides agreed to make future exercises more complex and include unmanned systems.They also agreed to strengthen cooperation between the Indian Navy and the Japan Maritime Self-Defence Force. This will cover maritime and air domain awareness, search and rescue operations, information sharing, and humanitarian assistance and disaster relief.The two countries also committed to improving mine-countermeasure capabilities and exploring joint development in naval shipbuilding and design.Singh said India and Japan had agreed to accelerate cooperation in niche underwater and missile technologies.Push for joint defence manufacturing and shipbuildingThe ministers discussed expanding defence industrial cooperation under the 'Design with Japan, Make in India' framework.They looked forward to early progress on the UNICORN project, which involves the co-development of integrated antenna masts for Indian Navy warships. The two sides also discussed India's Acceptance of Necessity (AoN) for the project by February 2027.Singh called for an early conclusion of a Maritime Ship Repair Arrangement (MSRA) to allow both countries to use each other's ship repair facilities.During his bilateral meeting with Koizumi on the sidelines of the 2+2 dialogue, Singh said there was considerable potential for cooperation in naval shipbuilding, unmanned and autonomous systems, advanced defence technologies and the wider defence industrial ecosystem.“I believe India and Japan have complementary strengths. We should be looking increasingly at joint development, manufacturing and long-term technological partnerships,” he said.Singh also highlighted progress since Koizumi's visit to India in August. This included the third India-Japan Defence Industries Forum, held in Tokyo on October 13, 2026, and a meeting of the Joint Working Group on Defence Equipment and Technology Cooperation.Economic security and supply chainsEconomic security was another key focus of the discussions. The joint statement expressed grave concern over economic coercion, including arbitrary export restrictions and non-market policies that create excess capacity and disrupt global supply chains.Although the statement did not name any country, the ministers called for a fair and competitive global environment and more reliable supply chains among like-minded partners.They agreed to promote cooperation in semiconductors, critical minerals, information and communication technology, clean energy and pharmaceuticals. They also called for closer engagement between governments, industries and research institutions to diversify supply chains and reduce strategic vulnerabilities.Jaishankar said the two countries had discussed the “growing tendency to weaponise connectivity, resources, services, supply chains and market shares.”He said many of these developments had direct implications for national security. “Strengthening resilience and exploring new options must be seen in that context.”Referring to experiences in West Asia, Jaishankar also flagged concerns over connectivity and maritime chokepoints.“Ensuring that maritime trade, which is at the heart of international commerce, functions smoothly is imperative. Our maritime cooperation can help make a difference,” he said.AI, cybersecurity and space cooperationIndia and Japan also agreed to expand cooperation in emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI), cybersecurity and space.The ministers recognised both countries as strategic research and development partners in AI and agreed to deepen cooperation under the Japan-India AI Cooperation Initiative (JAI).With cyberattacks becoming more frequent, they called for stronger collaboration on AI-enabled cybersecurity and the protection of AI systems, particularly those linked to critical infrastructure.They directed their teams to renew the existing Memorandum of Cooperation on Cybersecurity and hold the next India-Japan Cyber Dialogue at an early date.The two sides also agreed to work towards secure and resilient digital connectivity across the Indo-Pacific. This includes cooperation on trusted, high-speed and reliable undersea cable networks, as well as sharing best practices to protect critical undersea communications infrastructure.Cooperation in space situational awareness and the use of space-based assets for maritime domain awareness will also be expanded.Jaishankar said the discussions took into account the changing nature of warfare and the growing use of smart weapons and innovative solutions.India, Japan condemn cross-border terrorismThe joint statement strongly condemned terrorism and violent extremism in all forms, including cross-border terrorism.The ministers called for concerted action against all United Nations-listed terrorist groups and entities, including Al Qaeda, ISIS/Daesh, Lashkar-e-Tayyiba (LeT), Jaish-e-Mohammad (JeM) and their proxies.They also called for action to dismantle terrorist safe havens, cut off terror financing channels, break links between terrorism and transnational crime, and stop the cross-border movement of terrorists.Support for UN Security Council reformsIndia and Japan reiterated their support for reforming the United Nations Security Council, including expanding both permanent and non-permanent membership to reflect present-day geopolitical realities.Both countries expressed support for each other's bid for permanent membership in a reformed Council. They also confirmed mutual backing for each other's candidatures for non-permanent seats for the 2028-29 and 2033-34 terms.Indo-Pacific and Quad cooperationThe ministers reaffirmed their commitment to a free, open and rules-based Indo-Pacific, stressing respect for national sovereignty and territorial integrity and the peaceful resolution of disputes.They said countries should refrain from attempts to unilaterally change the status quo through threats or the use of force.The meeting also reviewed cooperation under the Indo-Pacific Oceans' Initiative (IPOI), India's MAHASAGAR vision and Japan's updated Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP) vision.The discussions came two days after the Quad leaders' summit in Manila, attended by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, US President Donald Trump, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.The ministers welcomed the November 2026 summit and recent Quad foreign ministers' meetings. They also discussed aligning bilateral cooperation with the Quad's priorities, including maritime security, economic prosperity, critical and emerging technologies, and humanitarian assistance.The two countries also highlighted the importance of working with ASEAN members to strengthen regional stability. They welcomed the first India-Japan-Philippines Trilateral 1.5 Dialogue and the first trilateral naval PASSEX exercise involving India, Japan and Indonesia.Jaishankar said the broader objective of India-Japan cooperation was to support a multipolar Asia and a multipolar world.75 years of diplomatic ties in 2027India and Japan will mark 75 years of diplomatic relations in 2027. The two countries have agreed to celebrate the occasion as the India-Japan Year of Shared Horizons.The fifth Coast Guard Global Summit will also be held in India in February 2027. Both sides agreed to organise a dialogue between their consular authorities.The next India-Japan 2+2 Ministerial Meeting will be held in India on a mutually convenient date.

articles.title: A powerful El Niño continues to strengthen ahead of Thanksgiving. Here’s what travelers need to know.
articles.summary: From wetter weather in Florida to potentially drier conditions in parts of the Caribbean, NOAA meteorologists explain what El Niño could mean for popular win...
articles.body:
With Thanksgiving a week away and El Niño still strengthening , holiday travelers face increased odds of stormy weather in parts of the South, while the Caribbean may stay drier.

The climate pattern, which occurs when waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean become unusually warm, can shift weather patterns across the country, potentially affecting popular winter getaways from Florida to the Caribbean.

NOAA's Climate Prediction Center said on Nov. 12 that El Niño is still strengthening, with a greater-than-79 % chance of a strong-to-very-strong event between January and March 2027. That's down from 83% in its October update, but it's still likely to produce adverse conditions, with wetter weather in the South and warmer weather in the North.

"El Niños are associated with more storminess across the southern tier of the country, and potentially more ice storms across the southern plains," Matthew Rosencrans, a meteorologist at NOAA's Weather Prediction Center, told Yahoo Travel in October.

Those conditions can significantly disrupt travel, the meteorologist said, but the effects will be far from uniform. El Niño winters are also often warmer, Rosencrans explains, which can sometimes benefit travel across the northern tier of the contiguous U.S.

Meanwhile, parts of the Caribbean may see drier weather, creating very different conditions for travelers depending on their destination.

NOAA's Climate Prediction Center outlook , released on Thursday, Nov. 19, said the strong El Niño will be the major influence on U.S. weather this winter, with wetter-than-normal conditions favored across the southern tier of the country and the Southeast. The outlook covers December through February rather than Thanksgiving week itself, but it points to a stormier backdrop for winter travel in the South.

Though slightly fewer people are expected to travel by car or plane for Thanksgiving this year, the AAA still expects 81.5 million people to travel at least 50 miles over the holiday. Bus, train and cruise travel is projected to increase.

No single storm is expected to disrupt travel nationwide before Thanksgiving, AccuWeather reports, but the most persistent wet weather will be in the Southeast, following heavy rain and flooding in Florida this week. Periods of rain and thunderstorms from the Gulf Coast into the Southeast early in the week could cause delays at major connecting hubs such as Atlanta and Charlotte, affecting travelers flying on to Florida and the Caribbean.

Return trips could be rougher, with conditions potentially becoming much stormier across much of the East right after the holiday.

Where winter travelers could feel the effects

Travelers heading to Florida this winter for a holiday getaway could face wetter-than-usual conditions, with El Niño increasing the likelihood of rainfall and severe weather across parts of the Southeast.

"For Florida, it often means a fairly robust secondary severe weather season in November and into December across the Southeast and Florida," Rosencrans says.

NOAA's outlook gives Florida, southern Georgia and the coastal Carolinas the greatest likelihood of a wetter-than-normal winter, with a greater than 70% chance of above-normal precipitation for December through February. Temperatures are expected to be near normal across parts of the Southeast, though forecasters note considerable uncertainty and say a shift in Atlantic air-pressure patterns, known as a negative North Atlantic Oscillation, could bring cooler spells.

That doesn't necessarily mean travelers need to rethink a Florida vacation, but those hoping for uninterrupted beach weather should keep an eye on the forecast.

While Florida could see a wetter winter, the Caribbean islands may see less rain, though it varies by island and time of year. Rosencrans said the Caribbean can often see drier weather during El Niño events, though the effect is strongest in summer.

The ABC islands (Aruba, Bonaire and Curaçao) are one example of where less rain is likely. Their main rainy season typically runs from October through January, with the dry season arriving later, from February through May. An El Niño suppresses that rainy season, according to the Meteorological Department of Curaçao .

While lower rainfall over the islands may sound appealing, Rosencrans says it can mean fewer thunderstorms and make days feel hotter "as there is less cloudiness and continuous sunshine."

How did El Niño affect hurricane season?

While El Niño suppressed Atlantic activity this year, the National Hurricane Center is now watching a possible late-season system off the Southeast coast this weekend, giving it a 60% chance of becoming a subtropical or tropical storm within seven days.

Lindsey Long, a meteorologist at NOAA's Weather Prediction Center, told Yahoo in October that, "in a typical year, we would expect about two additional hurricanes to develop between mid-October and Nov. 30."

The upcoming storm, which would be named Kyle, will affect the weather even if it doesn't develop further. Forecasters expect strong winds, dangerous surf and coastal flooding along parts of the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic coasts into the early part of Thanksgiving week.

Beyond this weekend's possible storm, the bigger risks for winter travelers are likely to be storms and delays rather than tropical systems.

NOAA's Climate Prediction Center expects El Niño to remain strong through the winter, peaking around the turn of the year, and to persist through spring before a shift to neutral conditions becomes more likely between April and June. The agency's next El Niño update is due on Dec. 10, with its next seasonal outlook following on Dec. 17.

Travelers heading to the South or the Caribbean may want to consider flexible booking options and check their travel insurance to see which weather-related disruptions are covered, including delays and cancellations caused by winter storms.

articles.title: Super El Niño will vanish by next hurricane season and that could spell danger
articles.summary: The end of Atlantic hurricane season is close. Next season could flip on its head with La Niña.
articles.body: The end is near for this remarkably suppressed Atlantic hurricane season, but forecasters are already sounding the alarm for next year, when super El Niño will likely be gone. This year’s only hurricane was Isaias; the last season with a single hurricane was 1925’s — 101 years ago. This is also the least active season in more than a decade, even if Kyle manages to form later this week. The Atlantic Ocean still tried. It quickly warmed enough to fuel powerful storms, but El Niño played the foil, generating constant storm-killing winds in the atmosphere. That meant, aside from Isaias, the storms that managed to find an opening to form were short-lived and weak. “It was an extremely powerful El Niño doing what extremely powerful El Niños do,” Phil Klotzbach, a hurricane expert at Colorado State University, told CNN. Every action has an equal but opposite reaction and powerful El Niños are no different. They often quickly flip to their counterpart La Niña and its much more favorable conditions for hurricanes the following year. A ‘sobering’ setup for 2027 A quick El Niño refresher: It is a natural climate cycle where warmer-than-average water along the equator in the Pacific Ocean creates a domino effect on global weather patterns. In this case, a slower Atlantic hurricane season and a supercharged Pacific one. This year’s El Niño, which already “super” strong, could wind up being the strongest on record when it peaks this winter. Stronger means its more likely to influence the weather, not necessarily make it more extreme. But just like weightlifters can only hold their heaviest weights for so long before their strength gives out, El Niño can’t maintain its intensity forever. The stronger the El Niño, the faster it loses its grip. “We tend to see a rapid weakening from winter into spring and summer,” after strong El Niños peak, Nat Johnson, a meteorologist at the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) explained. “They often crash hard.” NOAA’s latest forecast for El Niño, its cold counterpart La Niña and the near-normal or “neutral” conditions in between captures this crash out. El Niño is forecast to give way to neutral conditions by late spring or early summer, and La Niña may not be far behind. The forecast currently gives La Niña conditions about a 1 in 3 chance to emerge this upcoming summer. That’s a big deal because La Niña conditions usually offer the reverse of El Niño for the Atlantic hurricane season — less opportunity for storm killing winds, so more storms form and strengthen. And the earlier La Niña arrives, the wider the door is open for tropical activity. Those odds will likely fluctuate in the coming months, but forecasters have more confidence in La Niña’s ultimate arrival than normal because that’s the typical progression after strong El Niño events wind down, according to Johnson. The potential for a busy season doesn’t hinge on La Niña alone. With El Niño out of the way, neutral conditions can also sustain more storms, especially if water temperatures in the Atlantic start the season hotter than normal. Sea surface temperatures in the Atlantic are at or near record-breaking levels for November. The ocean will shed some of that heat in the winter and spring, but temperatures could still be juiced enough to fuel early storms when the next hurricane season begins on June 1. “We think the odds of a very busy hurricane season next year in the Atlantic are very high,” Klotzbach said, calling the setup “sobering.” Looking back at 2026 Early forecasts for this season — including Colorado State’s — called for below-average activity, with El Niño cited as the main factor. But the season underperformed even those tepid expectations. This one notched the fewest named storms – tropical storm or stronger – in a season since 2014, when only eight formed. Its 10 named storms are four less than average with minimal prospects until the season officially ends on November 30. Of those, six lasted 48 hours or less. Hurricane Isaias was a deadly exception. Isaias became a hurricane on October 8, which was the latest first hurricane in an Atlantic season on record, according to Klotzbach. Isaias’ timing also meant that the Atlantic didn’t have a single hurricane roaming the basin during its September peak for the first time since 1994. Isaias peaked at Category 3 strength in the Gulf before making landfall as a Category 2 on the Florida Panhandle on October 9. Authorities pinned the deaths of at least four people to Isaias as it tore through the South, dumping rain and bringing down trees and power lines along the way. Three short-lived tropical storms also made landfall along the Gulf Coast this season: Arthur, Bertha and Edouard. Arthur and Edouard brought gushing rainfall and intense flooding to parts of Louisiana and Texas, respectively. El Niño’s mark on the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season is indelible. Time will tell if its legacy also includes invoking a La Niña and a much busier hurricane season next year.

articles.title: How Joanne Young was drugged by husband and raped by strangers over 13 years
articles.summary: The warning comes after four men are found guilty of abusing a woman who was drugged by her husband.
articles.body:
Warning: This story discusses sexual violence and abuse

When Joanne Young awoke tied to her bed, she had no idea about the horror that had been unfolding while she was unconscious.

After hearing her then-husband Philip Young calling for someone else to "get down", she quickly realised another person was in the bedroom with them.

Unbeknown to Joanne, Young had advertised online for other men to abuse her. He then drugged her and invited a series of strangers into their bedroom to sexually assault her.

On Thursday, four men were convicted of a number of offences including raping and assaulting her . Her ex-husband had already pleaded guilty to a number of rape charges.

Young, a former Conservative councillor, and another man, Dean Hamilton, pleaded guilty to rape and sexual assault at a previous hearing.

The group came from a variety of backgrounds. One of the men worked on Ministry of Defence nuclear defence projects while another drove Red Cross trucks to Romania in the 1980s.

Speaking outside court after the verdicts earlier, Joanne said "silence is not an option if we are serious about preventing abuse" - you can read her statement in full here.

Her case has striking comparisons with the repeated rape of Gisèle Pelicot in France, with experts saying the crime was "deeply abusive".

Online, Young portrayed the abuse as a shared sexual kink known as "cuckolding". The photographs used in the adverts posted on sites like Craigslist and Grindr showed Joanne inanimate and tied to the bed.

James Foster, a specialist prosecutor with the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), said Young "would drug her so that he could then sexually abuse her and record that sexual abuse and also arrange for other men to attend the address to sexually abuse her".

One of the men who answered the advert was Dean Hamilton, 46, who admitted to raping Joanne and abusing her in 2015.

The other men who were convicted of sexually assaulting Joanne were Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, Richard Wilkins, 62, Norman Macksoni, 48 and Mohammed Hassan, 38 - the man Young told to "get down" when Joanne woke.

They told the court they believed they had the consent of both Joanne and Young and were told Joanne was pretending to be asleep - when in fact she was heavily sedated.

"But not once during any of this abuse did they ask Joanne Young what she wanted or show any interest in what her wishes were," Foster said.

The law states the sexual consent can only be given if the person involved "agrees by choice ... and has the freedom and capacity to make that choice".

Investigators are told to establish "what steps, if any, the suspect took to obtain the complainant's consent".

Professor Marianne Hester, emeritus professor at the University of Bristol, said Joanne "clearly" had no capacity to say no, adding a "women cannot consent if they are asleep".

"So it's the same if they are completely drugged. They cannot make the decision to agree to sex," she added.

Hester, who has researched gender-based violence for years, said those cases raise broader questions about attitudes towards women and sex.

"We have to question the men, the way men think it's okay to do sex and how they keep normalising, we keep normalising all these very abusive acts within sex and that's really problematic," she said.

Hester added: "We know that investigations have now started on certain websites and that individuals have been identified in a number of different countries who have been up to exactly the same kind of thing.

"So I think that there are potentially quite a lot more cases in the pipeline."

The case has also reignited questions about the role of websites used to facilitate abuse.

Lisa Sugiura, Professor of Cyber Crime and Gender at the University of Portsmouth, argued online platforms have a responsibility to address content that normalises violence against women.

"Often these sites are accompanied by image-based abuse and deeply violent language and rhetoric about women anyway," she said.

"You think, how are these forums allowed to act with impunity without oversight and accountability?

"Before we even get to the question of whether we should simply accept the word of a man claiming to speak on behalf of himself and his wife."

Data shows hundreds of similar potential crimes are currently being investigated across the UK.

The National Crime Agency said there was an "urgent need" to deal with the problem as an international issue.

NCA investigators have identified more than 270 individuals linked to one online forum and successor groups.

The CPS describes this type of offending as an emerging challenge for investigators.

"This particular type of offending, where a husband is drugging and abusing his wife and arranging for other men to abuse her, does seem to be a new type of offending," said Foster.

A spokesman for Wiltshire Police explained the extent of drug-rape offences was unknown because victims might not know they had been targeted.

He said: "While cases involving organised drug-facilitated sexual assault remain relatively rare compared to other forms of sexual offending, intelligence and other recent cases would suggest this may be a significantly under-reported crime type.

"Victims are often unaware they have been drugged, may have fragmented memories of events, or may initially attribute symptoms to alcohol consumption. These factors make detection and reporting particularly challenging."

Sugiura disagrees the offending itself is new.

She believes technology has made it easier to facilitate and conceal abuse that may have existed for years.

"The use of technology enables anonymity, it enables that division of identity, the protection of the respectable face offline, and these heinous deeds online," she said, adding offenders often operate within wider online communities where misogynistic attitudes are encouraged and abusive material is shared.

"These are not always isolated incidents," she said.

"They can be part of larger networks where people are swapping tips, encouraging one another and sharing material that is deeply abusive towards women."

"I think that there are potentially quite a lot more cases in the pipeline," she added.

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, support and information is available at BBC Action Line

articles.title: Museum's future at Shrewsbury Castle uncertain as review takes place
articles.summary: Shropshire Council is looking at a number of options for the future of Shrewsbury Castle.
articles.body:
A council review has left the future of a regimental museum at Shrewsbury Castle uncertain.

Shropshire Council said it wanted to see what repairs were needed and also put together a plan to make sure the castle remained financially viable.

The Soldiers of Shropshire Museum has been based at Shrewsbury Castle for more than 40 years and tells the story of Shropshire regiments going back to the 18th Century

Its lease is due to expire next May and the council said it was talking to the museum trustees who were considering the possibility of a move elsewhere.

The council has spent £1.8m to stabilise the crenelations and carry out other repairs, with more work required in the near future.

As a result there will be no programme of cultural events at the castle next summer.

Alex Wagner, the council's deputy leader, said the castle was a "fantastic tourist attraction" and the authority wanted to make sure it "remains a vibrant civic landmark".

Shropshire Council declared a "financial emergency" last year and in February it received promises of government loans totalling £192.8m to balance the books.

Wagner said any investment in the castle must "not just protect the asset for future generations but also make it a sustainable and viable asset for the future".

Reform UK councillor Brendan Mallon, who is a military veteran, asked for clarity from Shropshire Council at a cabinet meeting on Wednesday.

He said: "The museum's presence in the castle has been a very successful fit," adding that it was "highly appropriate" for it to remain.

Referencing rumours about the future use of the castle, he added: "The suggestion that the castle could instead become a wedding venue makes little commercial or practical sense."

Wagner said the council was in the process of commissioning an independent review to look at a range of options for the castle.

In the meantime, he said regular meetings were taking place with the museum trustees.

"We will continue to work with the Soldiers of Shropshire Trust as they continue to consider and refine their business plan and explore future possibilities - whether at Shrewsbury Castle or a suitable alternative location," he said.

This news was gathered by the Local Democracy Reporting Service which covers councils and other public service organisations.

articles.title: 'India has become a side player': Rahul attacks PM Modi's foreign policy, cites Pak's role in Iran-US talks
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi slammed Prime Minister Narendra Modi's foreign policy saying \"India has become a side player\" in global affairs,
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi slammed Prime Minister Narendra Modi's foreign policy saying "India has become a side player" in global affairs, while citing Pakistan's role in facilitating peace talks between the US and Iran.Speaking at an interaction with students at the University of Chicago on Wednesday (local time), Rahul said, "India, by its size, naturally has a global voice and India should be actively involved in global conversations. But frankly, India has become a side player.""I'm pretty shocked that Pakistan is busy negotiating with the Iranians and the Americans, and India's just looking," he added.The Lok Sabha leader of opposition said that India had played a prominent role in global affairs after Independence, particularly through the Non-Aligned Movement and expressed a desire to see New Delhi regain that stature.Rahul also questioned PM Modi's reliance on personal relationships with world leaders, including US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, arguing that diplomatic and geopolitical decisions could not be driven by individual equations."Friendship is not the point. Who gives a damn about friendship? Do you really think that geopolitics is going to work because the guy is your friend? He's leading a structure. He's got a whole economic system under him," Rahul said during the interaction, moderated by Professor Robert Pape."He's not going to make decisions based on whether he likes you or doesn't like you. So these are some of the things that disturb me,” he added.He clarified that he had no objection to leaders maintaining personal friendships, but said foreign policy should be guided by a clear understanding of national interests and India's position in the world."I don't have a problem with being friends with Mr Modi or being friends with leaders. Friendship is not that important. What's important is that you understand what's going on, who you are, and where you fit," he said."The next global architecture will not be built by one civilisation alone. It will be shaped by multiple civilisations, with America, China, India, the Middle East and Russia all having a role to play," he added.The remarks come amid renewed tensions in the Gulf, with diplomatic efforts to ease the US-Iran conflict facing setbacks. The earlier ceasefire and diplomatic framework have broken down, while negotiations remain stalled over differences on sanctions, the US naval blockade and the Strait of Hormuz.Responding to a question from a Pakistani participant on the possibility of improving bilateral ties, Rahul Gandhi said dialogue with Islamabad could begin if Pakistan stopped supporting and encouraging terrorism in India.Rahul said India could not engage in talks while innocent people continued to be killed in terror attacks allegedly backed by Pakistan."The moment that stops, a conversation can potentially begin," he said, adding that accepting such violence while maintaining dialogue was impossible for India.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Yalta format will not bring peace to Europe': Germany's Merz pans Xi-Putin-Trump trilateral
articles.summary: The world once watched three powerful leaders sit around a table at Yalta and shape the future of post-war Europe.
articles.body: The world once watched three powerful leaders sit around a table at Yalta and shape the future of post-war Europe. Nearly 81 years later, Germany fears a similar chapter could unfold again.As Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping meet in China amid the war in Ukraine, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has drawn a clear red line, warning that a "Yalta format will not bring peace to Europe" and insisting that Ukraine's future cannot be decided by major powers behind its back.According to Reuters, speaking at a press conference following the Coalition of the Willing meeting in Berlin on Thursday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Germany wanted Ukraine to secure "freedom that is rightful and lasting" and pledged to support Kyiv "for as long as needed".He also pointed to a broad European consensus on providing financial backing to Ukraine, underlining that continued support for Kyiv remained central to Europe's approach to the war.Taking a swipe at the Trump-Putin-Xi meeting in Shenzhen, Merz described the gathering as "above all a photo opportunity", questioning its significance in bringing an end to the war.He said Russia knew its maximalist demands were unrealistic and warned against any settlement that undermined Ukraine's sovereignty or Europe's security interests.On the possibility of easing pressure on Moscow, Merz said a conditional lifting of sanctions against Russia could be considered if meaningful progress was made towards peace. He also stressed that Washington could count on Germany's cooperation as long as both countries continued to share the same objectives.A meeting of the Coalition of the Willing was held in Berlin, bringing together Ukraine's main European allies as they sought a greater role in US-led efforts to end the war.According to Reuters, the gathering included the leaders of Germany, France, Britain, Poland and Italy, along with Nato secretary general Mark Rutte. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and US President Donald Trump's special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner also attended.The summit was jointly convened by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, French President Emmanuel Macron and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham.The meeting focused on coordinating diplomatic efforts, reaffirming support for Kyiv and discussing security guarantees that could come into force following a ceasefire. German officials said its timing was intended to allow European allies to respond jointly to developments from the Shenzhen summit.In Shenzhen, Trump, Putin and Xi held their first-ever trilateral meeting on Thursday, bringing together the leaders of the world's three largest nuclear powers for discussions on global security, nuclear arms control and the war in Ukraine.The meeting, held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, lasted around 70 minutes, according to the Associated Press.Trump said the three countries were "making history", while Putin highlighted their shared interests in resolving regional conflicts, including the war in Ukraine. Xi called for cooperation among the three major powers to maintain international peace and stability.Following the meeting, the three countries issued a joint declaration reaffirming that a nuclear war "cannot be won and must never be fought".The document also called for reforms to the United Nations, increased supplies of refined petroleum products and respect for the immunity of state officials in international courts.However, it offered no concrete breakthrough or roadmap for ending the Ukraine war, despite the conflict being discussed. Ukraine was also not represented at the trilateral meeting.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: ‘Not an acquittal’: After impeachment vote, Hegseth still under microscope
articles.summary: A week after a fizzled impeachment bid, analysts say Hegseth continues to face backlash for his leadership at Pentagon.
articles.body:
In the wake of the United States midterm elections, attention has turned to whether Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth will be able to preserve his cabinet-level position once Congress’s new Democratic majorities are sworn in.

Already, the Fox News host-turned-military-chief has faced mounting calls for his removal from office.

But analysts question the extent to which Hegseth’s impeachment would affect military policy under President Donald Trump.

“Ultimately, the secretary of defence is a powerful participant in shaping a war,” said Jasmine El-Gamal, a former Middle East adviser in the Pentagon.

El-Gamal, however, believes targeting Hegseth alone would not be enough to secure accountability for decisions like launching the US-Israel war on Iran.

Hegseth holds significant power in directing the US war effort, she explained, but he also works hand-in-hand with the president and his advisers.

“Calling him merely an ‘executor’ understates that power, while calling him its sole architect understates the president’s power and obscures where particular decisions were actually made,” El-Gamal said.

Since he was sworn in on January 25, 2025, Hegseth has overseen some of Trump’s most controversial international campaigns, including the war on Iran and a series of deadly boat strikes in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific Ocean.

Both campaigns have been accused of violating international law. The Iran war, in particular, became a political albatross for Trump’s Republican Party during the midterm race.

A poll earlier this month found that 44 percent of US voters said they were less likely to vote for a midterm candidate who supported the war.

That number dwarfed the 13 percent who said they were more inclined to vote for such a candidate, by a ratio of more than three to one.

The Democratic Party scored a thumping victory in the November 3 midterms, flipping both the House of Representatives and the Senate from Republican control.

Less than a week later, Hegseth faced a push for impeachment, led by outgoing Republican Congressman Thomas Massie.

Among the eight articles of impeachment Massie filed were accusations that Hegseth had dismantled fundamental safeguards to protect civilian lives, leading to incidents like the bombing of an elementary school in Minab, Iran, that killed at least 120 children.

But the impeachment proceedings were shelved on November 10, after the Republicans’ lame-duck majority in the House voted 211 to 204 to block the measure. Eleven Democrats were absent for the vote.

Hegseth is hardly the first Pentagon chief to face pressure to leave office following a dismal election for his party.

In November 2006, Republicans likewise suffered a midterm rout amid a groundswell of voter ire over the US-led wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. Both chambers of Congress that year flipped to Democratic control.

Within a day of the vote, then-President George W Bush announced that his defence secretary, the late Donald Rumsfeld , would resign. He cited the Iraq war in his remarks.

“I recognise that many Americans voted last night to register their displeasure with the lack of progress being made there,” Bush said of the conflict.

Hegseth, however, has resisted calls for his resignation. In a five-minute video posted two days after the midterms, Hegseth dismissed his critics as “deep-state radicals” obsessed with “political theatre”.

“They attack us because we are effective. It’s not going to work. We will not back down,” Hegseth said. “We put America and the war-fighter first, always and without apology. And that fight continues in the lame-duck Congress.”

His message of defiance included an appeal for the military to “stay the course”, including in the war against Iran.

“I’ll assure you, we have only just begun to fight,” Hegseth added. “We are more determined than ever, more resolute than ever to finish what we have started.”

Some of the criticism, however, has come from within Hegseth’s own party. Vice President JD Vance, for instance, said the “real reason” the Republicans lost the midterms is “obvious to almost everyone”.

“The reason we lost is the war,” he wrote on social media.

Hala Rharrit, a former US diplomat who spent 18 years in the State Department, was among the officials who resigned before Trump took office for his second term, in protest of the US involvement in Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza .

She explained that Hegseth would have been critical in guiding some of the Iran war’s most divisive moments.

The bombing of the Minab elementary school, for example, took place on February 28, the first day of the conflict.

Rharrit said Hegseth and other senior Department of Defense (DOD) officials would have drawn up the initial strike lists before advising Trump on the targets for final approval.

“I suspect that Trump would not get into the granularities of which targets to strike on day one,” Rharrit told Al Jazeera.

“Hegseth and others in DOD had a lot to do with those precise decisions, which also runs through lawyers.”

She also drew a line between decisions taken by Hegseth and Trump and the losses the US and its allies have endured since the war began.

Iran has retaliated against US and Israeli attacks with strikes across the Middle East. At least 23 US service members have died in the conflict, and 865 were wounded.

“Ultimately, they are both responsible, not just for the strikes in Iran, but also for making American service members and diplomats throughout the region sitting ducks,” said Rharrit.

Throughout the war, Congress has had the power to pull the emergency cord and stop the fighting, according to Brian Finucane, who served as a legal adviser in the State Department from 2011 to 2021.

Under the Constitution, “the overwhelming bulk of war powers belong” to the members of Congress, he said.

He sees the midterm results, in part, as a backlash to the Trump administration’s expansive use of executive power.

After all, critics say officials like Hegseth have offered Congress relatively little transparency in the military’s overseas actions.

“We’ve seen sort of the apex of presidential unilateralism under Trump,” Finucane said. “I think it has reminded Americans of why the Constitution gives Congress, not one man, the power to take the country to war.”

The incoming Democrat-led Congress has pledged to use its power to check Trump’s war-making powers and confront Hegseth over his policies.

In the final days of the midterm race, Democratic Congressman Hakeem Jeffries , who is now in line to become the first Black speaker of the House , told supporters that Hegseth’s days were numbered.

“In the majority, one of the first things we’re going to do is run Pete Hegseth out of town,” Jeffries said.

He has since described himself as a “hard yes” on impeachment proceedings against the Pentagon chief.

But El-Gamal cautioned against treating the impeachment vote as the only path to accountability.

“Impeachment is just one constitutional accountability mechanism,” said El-Gamal.

She pointed to congressional investigations and the legislature’s “power of the purse” — its authority over federal spending — as two other avenues for reining in Hegseth and Trump.

El-Gamal added that November’s blocked impeachment motion “was not an acquittal nor a vote resolving the allegations” of war crimes in Iran and elsewhere. She anticipates the new Congress, once sworn in, will continue to pursue those allegations.
